newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Price setting adds to Nigerian cement woes.
newsitem.headline: Price setting adds to Nigerian cement woes.

text.p: Nigerian cement companies, already suffering big sales drops, could face a tougher future as a government peg on cement prices erode their profits further, industry officials and analysts say.
Leading cement manufacturers have reported falling profits in their recent financial statements, causing their share prices to fall.

West African Portland Cement Company (WAPCO), the sectoral leader, posted a sharp drop in after-tax profit in 1996 from 1995, netting 1.8 billion naira in the year ended December 1996 against 3.1 billion naira in the year earlier.
Ashaka Cement Company in its latest quarterly result to end-February 1997 showed after-tax profit fell to 121.9 million naira from 160.7 million naira in 1996 period.
Analysts blamed the poor showing on increasing cost of production, adding that transportation and electricity bills were becoming prohibitive.
WAPCO's price has started to fall and it traded at 65.40 naira on Wednesday from this year's high of 65.50 naira.
Ashaka is suffering a worse fate, trading at 13.77 naira from its high this year of 16.50 naira.
The decision last year to fix the price of a bag of cement at 350 naira ought to be reviewed to prevent a collapse of the companies, said Farouk Umar, a director at Ashaka.
Umar said while the measure was hurting them, retailers were benefitting by selling above the fixed price in the market.
When finance minister Anthony Ani pegged the price last year, he said it was to make the product available at an affordable rate following concessions government gave local producers.
The government had complained that cement prices had not fallen even after it delayed until this year its decision to ban the import of gypsum, a major component in cement production.
Stock traders said cement shares would remain depressed for some time because of the current development in the sector, and as a result of a current bearish trend on the Nigerian stock market.
"Blue chips which until recently were considered untouchable are now on offer and we don't know for how long," one said.
There is no indication that the government will review its cement policy in the short term.

Industries minister Lieutenant-General Mohammed Haladu told manufacturers last week to enforce the the government price instead of complaining that cement was selling at a higher price in the open market.
He said at Ashaka that the government was determined to protect the public interest and that cement companies also had a responsibility to the nation.
